newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt says peace efforts need Israeli change. [CORRECTED 17:07 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Egypt says peace efforts need Israeli change. [CORRECTED 17:07 GMT]

text.p: Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said on Thursday Israeli policy on the Middle East peace process must change for his country's efforts to kickstart stalled peace talks to succeed.

A senior aide to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said on Wednesday that Egyptian efforts to revive Israeli-PLO peace talks were near collapse and complained that Washington had withdrawn from peacemaking.

Arafat stopped over in Cairo briefly on Thursday to discuss with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak the Middle East peace process, which has been in deep freeze since Israel began building a new settlement in Arab East Jerusalem in March.
"We must knock on all doors to save the peace process if Egyptian efforts to confront the deterioration are to continue. This needs a change in Israeli policies," Moussa said (corrects translation).

"Both sides must have clearly defined intentions in order to facilitate the continuation of the political work aimed at saving peace," he told reporters after meeting Saudi Arabian Foreign Minister Saud al-Faisal.

"The settlement policy and the retreat from what was agreed upon at Madrid (Middle East peace conference in 1991) and what was agreed upon in Oslo (peace talks in 1993) points to the danger of the crisis."
Peace talks between Israel and the Palestinians collapsed after the Jewish state began building the Jerusalem settlement.
Egypt has stepped in as the main mediator between the two sides over the past few weeks as a result of what many Arabs perceive as a lack of U.S. interest in the peace process.

Mubarak has sent his senior political adviser, Osama el-Baz, to see Palestinian and Israeli leaders several times in an attempt to bring them back to the negotiating table but both sides say there is still a gap between their positions.
Mubarak said Egypt would not for the time being resume its negotiating efforts but that contacts between the two sides would bring about progress soon.

But Ahmed Abdel-Rahman, secretary-general of the Palestinian Authority, on Wednesday blamed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for the failure of an Egyptian mediation drive and warned the West Bank and Gaza were on the verge of an explosion.

Arab anger has risen in the divided town of Hebron after the discovery on storefronts on Saturday of anti-Moslem hate posters depicting the Prophet Mohammad as a pig, an animal viewed as unclean by Islam.

"The distribution of posters offensive to Islam and its sacred symbols shows the extremism of Jewish settlers. Talk of security for settlers is the wrong way around. Securing Palestinians against extremism should be examined," said Moussa.
He said Israel should follow through after its apology with preventive measures so that such incidents do not recur.
Israeli troops on Wednesday wounded 37 youths protesting against the posters. Soldiers shot dead an Arab teenager in a clash in Gaza.
Israeli leaders have apologised to Palestinian political and religious officials for the posters, which Israeli police say were pasted by a 25-year-old Jewish woman from Jerusalem, now under arrest.
